title: Emergent Loop Geometry in Gauge-Equivariant Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Gauge-equivariant graph neural networks generate ordered products of gauge links through local message passing, but the geometry of these internal structures is not captured by the receptive field alone. We investigate the statistical ensemble of closed lattice walks generated by recursive node- and edge-feature operations, independently of network training. Analytical and numerical results reveal a separation between rapid growth of contour length and much slower spatial expansion: deeper compositions generate increasingly long paths through repeated traversal of relatively compact regions. Loop expansions of fermionic observables provide a physical interpretation of this hierarchy, showing how spatial locality remains compatible with high-order dependence on nearby gauge fields. These findings identify complementary roles of network depth in extending spatial reach and enriching the representations constructed within that reach, providing a geometrical perspective on learning lattice gauge observables.
summary: This work analyzes the geometry of paths generated by gauge-equivariant Graph Neural Networks operating on lattice gauge theory configurations. It finds that while the total path length can grow exponentially, the actual spatial area explored grows much more slowly. This reveals a fundamental distinction between path traversal order and physical spatial extent in these complex quantum models.
main_problem: The study investigates the geometry of internal structures generated by gauge-equivariant graph neural networks (GNNs) when processing gauge links, noting that the receptive field alone is insufficient to capture the full geometric complexity.
main_result: A clear separation exists between the rapid, exponential growth of the path's contour length and the much slower growth of its actual spatial extent, indicating repeated traversal of compact regions.
method: The analysis involves studying the statistical ensemble of closed lattice walks generated by recursive node- and edge-feature operations, independently of the network's training process.
model_or_system: The model is based on lattice gauge theories (like QCD) simulated on a lattice, where information is encoded in gauge links ($U_{ij}$) and processed via gauge-equivariant message passing within a GNN framework.
key_observables: Contour length ($\ell$), Radius of Gyration ($	ext{Rg}$), Number of Distinct Visited Sites ($N_{	ext{distinct sites}}$), and Effective Dimension ($D_{	ext{eff}}$).
important_parameters: Network depth (recursion depth $n$), spatial dimension ($d=2, 3, 4$), and the underlying gauge group structure.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the path generation process can be decoupled from the final non-linear processing steps, allowing for the study of the underlying path connectivity.
figures_summary: Figure 8 plots geometric observables ($	ext{Rg}$, $N_{	ext{distinct sites}}$, $D_{	ext{eff}}$) against loop length ($\ell$) for various dimensions and recursion depths, showing that spatial metrics grow much slower than the path length.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the GNN framework for gauge links, then analyzes the recursive path generation process, and finally compares the resulting path length statistics (contour length vs. spatial metrics) to reveal the geometric hierarchy.
why_interesting: The concept of path complexity and geometric constraints emerging from local interactions (like message passing) has parallels in understanding entanglement structure or correlation functions in many-body quantum systems.
